Sir, I said just now, during eighteen years Canada was stagnant and still ; had practically made no increase at all for the increase of two per cent per annum during these years can hardly be considered as anything worth taking seriously into *accovmt, and that both as respects the present growth of the population and as respects the growth and volume of our trade, It is absolutely and literally true that we are advancing now almost as fast, in one year as we were doing before in ten years.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright).

speechtext:
What was the policy that my friend Mr. Mackenzie desired to inaugurate i I have alluded to it before and may repeat it now. Mr. Mackenzie pushed forward with all his power the construction of the essential link between the waters of the great lakes and Winnipeg; he pushed forward, with all his energy, the surveys which it was absolutely necessary to make if the Canadian Pacific Railway was to be constructed at all, but, above all and before all, Mr. Mackenzie had placed before him the necessity of establishing, in the case of Manitoba,

a strong central province from which the Canadian Pacific Railway would radiate east and west as occasion demanded, and I say here now, having fully considered the whole situation, 1 say here now, with the additional experience of the last five and twenty years, that I fully believe that had Mr. Mackenzie's policy been carried out, had he remained in office, that Manitoba and the North-west Territories at least would have been as far advanced in 1885 as it is to-day in 1903. What we are doing now is practically, and literally almost, to repair the shortcomings which were committed during these eighteen years, and it is not an Insignificant thing, it is not a slight thing, that the very track of these railways that we are now considering goes as nearly as possible over the line which had been selected five and twenty years ago by Mr. Mackenzie, and which I well believe the gentlemen of the Canadian Pacific Railway regret exceedingly that they had not been required to adopt themselves.
Now, Sir, we have had placed before us two schemes; there is the scheme of my right hon. friend the First Minister, and there is the scheme of the hon. leader of the opposition. With respect to that, I might say with some degree of truth that whereas the hands are hands of Esau, the voice is the voice of Jacob. My hon. friend, peradventure, had been instructed-I will not say dry-nursed, as he objects to that phrase-he had been instructed apparently by my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) in propounding that scheme to the House. There are two or three things that strike one forcibly on looking at that scheme. I had not the advantage of hearing my hon. friend, but I read what I believe is a correct report of his speech. One suggestion that occurred to me was this, that as Canada east of Montreal had practically ignored my hon. friend and his followers, lie thought it would be a good piece of policy to ignore Canada east of Montreal. That was not natural, but I do not know that it was good policy. Looking at the whole scheme, according to such lights as I possess, it struck me forcibly that the leader of the opposition, whatever else he *might or might not have done, had certainly supplied my right hon. friend beside me with a very excellent argument in favour of his scheme. So far as I could see, the hon. gentleman proposed to spend a great deal more than would be necessary for us to spend, on any fair construction of the contract we are* making with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. He proposed to spend a great deal more than my right hon. friend beside me proposes to spend, and he likewise proposes to get a great deal less for our money. If I followed him correctly, he wants to buy a large portion of the *Canadian Pacific Railway line, which he would not get for nothing ; he also proposes
to double-track it-a somewhat expensive operation-he is willing to purchase the Canada Atlantic Railway, and I suppose doubletrack and improve that, also an expensive operation. He has views at some convenient time, not stated, but which he might find would come upon him soon, of building a railway along the height of land, too. I am told he is willing to expend a very large sum of money for the purpose of constructing and owning and operating also-an expensive amusement, I may venture to state-the section of road from Port Simpson or some other point on the coast to the edge of the Rocky mountains, and lie will likewise, I believe, be prepared to provide for the railways that would be required for the development of the prairie section. Take it all in all, I am inclined to think that for one penny my right hon. friend's scheme would cost, the plan of the leader of the opposition would cost us ten. However, that is a matter which we can discuss or which has been discussed already, and will be further discussed, on another occasion.
Now, Sir, with respect to our policy, I would like to point out to the hon. gen, tlemen opposite that there is more than one object to be aimed at in this project which is now before the House. Our objects are threefold : we desire in the first place-and that, of course, lies at the base of the scheme we are proposing to the House-to develop, and develop early, the whole of the North-west. We desire, in the second place, to knit together, as far as in us lies, the several sections of this Dominion ; and in the third place, to prevent the diverting of traffic, which unless some such project as this can be carried into effect, is almost certain to occur, I believe to the very considerable detriment of the i>eople of Canada.
Now, under these circumstances and granting that these are worthy ends, worthy of a great party, and a policy to be desired in itself, there are two questions to be asked of us : first of all, can we afford it under the circumstances, and, in the second place, is this the best method. Here, Sir, I will pause for one instant to review an argument preferred by an hon. gentleman on the other side. Now, I hate discussing these questions from a sectional standpoint. I think that in a federated commonwealth like ours, that is the very worst policy ; we must view these questions as a whole, as they will affect all Canada, not as they will affect one or two sections, however important. But if it is necessary to have regard to sectional arguments, and if my hon. friends opposite ask what Ontario is to gain under this project, I must for-once answer them according to their own line of argument. I say Ontario has a great deal to gain under this project. I say, Sir, speaking as an Ontarian, that, in the first place, about 1,000 miles of this projected

railway are to be constructed through the northern portion of Ontario, no insignificant advantage, on the whole, to that province. I say, in the second place, that the construction of that road on the terms on which we propose to construct it will bring almost every town and village of the smallest Importance in Ontario into direct communication with the whole of the Northwest Territories. I say, Sir, in the third place, if there should be any foundation at all for the statement made, apparently on good authority, by the government of Ontario, that the construction of this railway will open, to the advantage of the province and of the Dominion a very large and important section of territory in Ontario, which otherwise might remain for a whole generation lockedrup and useless. Sir, if I correctly followed the hon. gentleman who spoke last, I would judge that he approves of about 75 per cent of our scheme. If I followed him correctly, he would find no fault, I think he said he would find no fault, with the construction of this road from North Bay to the coast of the Pacific. It is not very often that a great project can be brought forward by one party and exposed to the criticisms of the other and get as many as 75 per cent good marks. It is some time since I stood my examination in the hall of any college, but if I recollect aright, in my days a gentleman with 75 per cent on his papers generally got first-class honours.
The true objection, although the hon. gentlemen opposite do not dwell very much upon that phase of it, the true objection as far as I could judge and I do not pretend to be a thought reader, that they had to this bargain of ours was that it was too good a one. They would have preferred we should have brought down a vey much worse one. Some of them hinted broadly-and I think inconsiderately-that the bargain is so good, they do not believe that the Grand Trunk Railway will ever live up to it. Well, I am not one of those who believe it to be necessary, in order that a bargain be a good one, that the other party to it should be defrauded or injured in any shape or way. I believe that a really good bargain may be one which is to the advantage of both parties. I think that this is notably an instance of the sort. The Grand Trunk Railway could not finance conveniently a transcontinental railway on its own resources. Strong as may be the hold, it undoubtedly has on a large section of the English public, I think that is rather beyond its power, and the government guarantee is worth many millions to it, if not absolutely indispensable. On the other hand, I equally strongly believe that the government, by the terms it has made, by the mode in which it proposes to deal with this great question, is likely to escape from a sea ot difficulties. Sir, were the government to own and operate, as has been suggested, Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
this transcontinental railway, and in particular to own and operate a section so remote as that west of Winnipeg, there would be no end to the demands that would almost of necessity be made upon it for the construction of branches here, there and everywhere, for the lowering of rates, and for concessions in every possible shape and form. I have seen enough in my time of government management of railways, and I do not hesitate to say that, in the present condition of Canada at any rate, under the form of government which subsists in Canada at any rate, it would be highly impolitic and prejudical to the best interests of the country for the government to own and operate a great system of railways. So far our experiments have been costly and not altogether satisfactory; and although I could understand that, under certain and totally different conditions, the policy of government ownership might be a fair subject for discussion. I beg leave to say that, as a rule, if the government is to own and operate railways, it must own and operate them all. I beg leave further to say that our present system of government is one which imposes no end of difficulties in the way of the successful operation of railways.
Not to take the proposition exactly of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, but to take the proposition advanced by several of his followers, what would we have if we had stopped at North Bay V Given the desirability of having an all-Oan-, adian route, it is plain that we have taken the only possible way in which that can be attained. In this business, I hold that it is idle, and worse than idle, to discuss the commercial side alone. While 1 grant that that is a very important side of it, still after all it is but one side of a great national question like this. That is the greatest difficulty which besets us in the task of opening up and settling and consolidating the various sections of this Dominion. Every man who has traversed that country, or who has examined the map, will agree that the greatest practical and pressing difficulty in the matter of consolidating the interests of the various portions of Canada, lies in the huge gap we have to bridge which extends from the borders of Manitoba nearly to the province of Quebec. At this moment that bridge, as it was described lately by Sir William Van Horne, can only be traversed by one single track railway. The difficulty is accentuated by the fact that there is a large influx of immigrants coming in from the; United States. In many respects those are the choicest we can get, the very best settlers that can come in. They are men of experience and capital, who will not be daunted by a single frost or disaster. They are, in every respect perhaps but one, the very best immigrants that can be had. One thing too may be said of them, that a very large number are men or descendants of men who, in former years, left Canada, and whom we

will be all delighted to welcome back to our territories. But while that is perfectly true, we must also remember that these men, from the necessity of the case, unless they are provided speedily with rapid means of communication, will tend to throw their traffic and commerce southward instead of eastward. That everybody will admit, and the circumstances are such that it is comparatively easy for them to do it. That, in my opinion, is the justification for the government of Canada incurring very considerable expense and taking very considerable risk for the purpose of securing as soon as we can, and on the best terms we can, another line of railway communication from older Canada to the new settlements. If we can create settlement along that new line, as there is reasonable hope we may do, no doubt we can go a very long way towards overcoming these difficulties. But my right hon. friend was perfectly right when he said time presses. At the best it will be some years before we can put this railway of ours into operation. In the meantime, population is pouring into the west, I am happy to say, at the rate of from 100,000 to 150,000 per year, and there is every reasonable probability that they will continue to do so (if they find railway facilities are being provided for them) during the next four on five years. At this moment, although a very large number of the immigrants who have come in have hardly had, time to break the sod, the resources of the two systems, which are now operating in the North-west, are taxed, as everybody knows, to the utmost to meet the demands of the settlers. What will they be five years hence when five hundred thousand or six hundred thousand of additional settlers will have found their way to the prairies of the Saskatchewan or the Peace river valley ? It is impossible for us to entirely prevent the tendency of trade to go south, and it would be absurd for us to attempt to prohibit it, but we have it in our power to provide other channels, and for this purpose, the aid of the Grand Trunk Railway is likely to be invaluable. For this purpose, we require, as in former days, the Canadian Pacific Railway required, to establish a system bringing our new line into communication with the majority of the people of Canada. Any man who knows anything of the history of the Canadian Pacific Railway knows that it was in the greatest difficulties until it had supplied itself with a system, such as the Grand Trunk Railway now has ready made; and my right hon. friend never showed his statesmanship better than when he seized the opportunity which the Grand Trunk Railway placed in his hand-the opportunity of securing the aid of a going concern with ramifications extending throughout the Dominion. Why, at the very outset a great volume of trade will be supplied to this new line of railway, which could be obtained by no other means whatever.
And, there is another consideration which it may be as well for the House to bear in mind. The Grand Trunk Railway has numerous connections. It is already extended to Chicago; and if we were to refuse to cooperate with it, if we were to refuse to accept the hand which is stretched out to us, the Grand Trunk Railway, beyond all question, would find its way into Manitoba and the North-west, but not through Canadian territory.
I do not know whether my friends opposite, I do not know whether my friends beside me, have appreciated the full significance of this fact, that, as the crow flies, the distance from Winnipeg to Chicago is just 700 miles, if the Grand Trunk so desired, it would be quite possible for it to obtain a very easy and effective entrance into the North-west through American territory. It is quite true-and there is the advantage we possess-that in any such attempt as that it would be impossible to get aid from us for the construction of a transcontinental railway. But, I repeat that if we do not choose to accept the offer they make, we should only have ourselves to blame, and we could not reasonably pass censure upon them if they avail themselves of their present connections and run their line to the North-west in that way.
Let me review the objections which my hon. friends opposite have brought forward. Those objections, as I took them down are in brief as follows :	They demand that
we shall have surveys and that we shall take more time. They allege though, I think, inconsiderately and without fairly estimating the value of the concessions which have been made to us by the Grand Trunk, that the price is much too high. They allege that we ignore great centres of commerce. Some allege that this road should be owned all through by the government, some that it should be owned and operated all through by the government. Now, Sir, as I have said, I was one of those who, two and thirty years ago, took part in the debates on the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Unfortunately, there are few left to bear witness to what took place then, but I assure the House that we know at the very least, a thousand times more of the route we are proposing to traverse than did the gentlemen who agreed, in 1871, to build the Canadian Pacific Railway within a period of ten years. Why, Sir, it took ten years before they could find a practicable route through British Columbia; and it is my profound belief that, as the late lamented Sir John A. Macdonald did not know, when he made the treaty of Washington, whether lie had the right to navigate the Yukon or not, so neither he nor his colleagues, when they made that bargain with British Columbia, knew whether they would have to cross one ridge of mountains or twenty. Certainly, surveys should be made, and they will be made and are being made; and most as-
That is rather rough on some of the right hon. gentleman's colleagues who read newspaper extracts.

I have not noticed that my hon. friends read newspaper extracts. But, I have here an opinion from a Conservative journalist and a gentleman who, I believe, gave a considerable amount of trouble to some of my friends at the recent election.
I will read what a Conservative journalist and aj Conservative speaker of considerable merit, I believe, had to say in respect to my right hon. friend's scheme. That gentleman writes :
_ The inhabitants of the territories would he justified in welcoming the Grand Trunk if for one reason only. That reason, which stands out. to my mind, in bold and convincing relief is that not one of the burdens or abuses which the territories have complained of in the Canadian Pacific Railway charter are to he found in the Grand Trunk proposal.
If the territories were asked to contribute of their remaining wild lands to the Grand Trunk, then might we well pause, and ask ourselves whether we were not paying too great.' a price for the road. But the territories do not give an acre. There is no cash bonus ; and the territories do not give a dollar. We shall have the Grand Trunk with spur lines and branch

lines opening up the country north and south of it ; rye shall have the evil spell of monopoly and one-road ascendancy broken absolutely without any first cost to ourselves. With another outlet to the two oceans, and the control of the rates in the hands of the government, should we not be even as the ass that brayeth, if we troubled ourselves very much about the Intercolonial, or hybridization, or any such secondary matters ? Truly we should.
If there were any exemption from taxes we might have cause to kick vigorously. But there is no tax exemption. The Grand Trunk will come in as a great taxpayer. It will contribute its share to the expense of schools and roads and bridges. Instead of being a legalized pirate, preying on the labour of the people, it will be a help to school districts, local improvement districts, and to towns and villages. This seems to me an important consideration ; and who in the territories would like to assume tho responsibility of keeping out this company which will help develop the country as a taxpayer as well as a common carrier.
If the Grand Trunk were receiving a cash bonus, then we in the territories might complain, and say we had given enough of our lands to the Canadian Pacific Railway and other railroads, without paying a toll of cash to tho Grand Trunk. But as before said, the territories pay not one dollar.
If tho Grand Trunk were coming into the territories with power to impose whatever rates it chose on the people of the territories, then I would indeed be the first to call a halt, till the people had protection. But the Grand Trunk will not be like the Canadian Pacific Railway. It will not have a free hand and a cloudy charter under which it can demand whatever tale of brick it chooses to levy. There will be government control of rates.
If the Grand Trunk were coming in with a monopoly of any kind we might well consider whether we had not just cause to look with suspicion on its advent. But it has no monopoly. No disallowance agitation will ever be necessary.
The Grand Trunk Pacific will, in my humble opinion, be a boon to Canada at large, and to no part of Canada more than to the territories. As an old resident of the territories I welocme it as the best and most encouraging event that has ever crossed the horizon of tho prairie country ; and if I might venture one word of advice to my fellow residents in the territories it is that they study the matter on its merits, and refuse to allow any mere question of party to influence them when the development, and to a large extent the whole future, of the territories are in the balance.
For if we do not get this road, what is there in sight that will do one tithe as much for us as we may reasonably expect from this new trunk road?
I think, Sir, that testimony, from a consistent opponent of the government, both with his pen and with his voice, is not to he entirely disregarded.

I dare say my hon. friend (Mr. Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
Davis) knows something of him. I think he has heard from Mr. Hawkes of the delinquencies of the present government on more than one occasion, as I have knowledge. Now, Sir, as I have said, given these conditions, it appears to me that the future of the North-west is reasonably assured. It appears to me that every cent we may expend we are justified in believing we will have returned to the public treasury tenfold by the policy we have entered into. If the scheme is carried out on the lines we have laid down, then, Sir, I venture to say that before five years have expired, by the end of which time we expect a large proportion of this road will be in active operation, the trade and commerce of this country will have increased, thanks to the production which we may reasonably expect to follow, to such a degree that the duties we will receive on our additional imports will probably in one single year more than implement the entire sum we will require to lay out on this road. And, Sir, in conclusion let me say, that if in 1871, when the revenue of Canada amounted to barely $20,000,000, when the trade and commerce of Canada collectively amounted to barely $17,000,000, we might have had cause to hesitate before we committed^ ourselves to a project Involving a gift of $100,000,000 for the construction of a little over 2,000 miles of road, it does not follow, that in 1903 when the trade and commerce of Canada amounted to $440,000,000 in place of $17,000,000 and the revenue to $66,000,000, in place of $20,000,000 we cannot afford to donate $14,000,000 for the construction of a road 3,500 miles in length.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not rise with the hope of saying anything new in this debate, because the question under discussion lias been dealt with from all standpoints. But tho position I have occupied and the attention that I have endeavoured to give to the transportation question make it a duty forme to ask the indulgence of the House on this occasion. One thing is cheering. We have not heard anybody during this long and interesting debate talking blue ruin or talking about the absence of the credit of this country. On both sides lion, members of tire House have expressed the fullest confidence in the future of Canada and in its ability to grapple with the biggest problems. Mr. Speaker, we possess in the North-west Territories a vast and fertile domain. Last year 100,000,000 bushels of grain of all kinds were grown in those territories, 53,000,000 bushels of wheat in Manitoba, and 14,000,000 bushels of wheat in the territories. During the last couple of years we have heard a good deal about the condition of trade in the west. Complaints have been made to this parliament over and over again. It was said that there were not enough elevators, not enough granaries either in the Territories or at the ter-

minals. The railways had not foreseen the great development that was coming on. They had not supplied themselves with the equipment which they could have, perhaps, provided. Undoubtedly, there was, as I have said, not enough elevators, not enough granaries, and undoubtedly there was not enough rolling stock at the disposal of the rail-way companies. The congestion existed from the wheat fields to the outlets. There was no congestion from the outlets to the seaboard. About the same congestion took place in the American territories, not quite to the same extent, but a good deal of congestion took place there. The evils of others do not cure our own. I fully recognize, and all men who have given some attention to the condition of affairs in this country have recognized that something ought to be done. I do not share the views of some of our colleagues in this parliament when they say that there has been no question of another transcontinental railway. The question was discussed in the press. It was discussed, specially, perhaps, in the province of Quebec, where the Trans-Canada Railway Company was organized four or five years ago, with the object of constructing a transcontinental railway. However, I do not mean to discuss that side of the question now. Let me call to the attention of parliament the geographical position of Canada. Our North-west Territories are tributary to Lake Superior, differing in that respect from the American states or from a good many of them at any rate. Some of the American states are tributary to Lake Superior, some others are tributary to Lake Michigan, and some others are tributary to the Gulf of Mexico. Our territories are tributary exclusively from the water-way standpoint to Lake Superior. We have no share in the ownership of Lake Michigan. During the last ten or twelve years the tendency of the grain and flour traffic has been towards Lake Superior. 'The construction of the Minneapolis, St. Paul and Sault Ste. Marie Railway which was completed in 1888, contributed greatly to make Duluth and West Superior more and more the head centres of the grain trade. Let me quote from the ' Monthly Summary of Commerce and Finance ' of the United States :
Spring wheat markets, reporting for eleven months, including Minneapolis, Milwaukee, Duluth, and Chicago, have thus far this year received 162,675,462 bushels, against 172,717,364 bushels in 1902 and 146,508,740 bushels in 1901. A marked feature in the wheat trade of the North-west is the concentration of the crop at Minneapolis and Duluth, at the former point for milling and at the latter for lake shipment eastward. More than half of the total receipts have gone to Minneapolis, and there is a steadily increasing volume drawn to that centre of consumption. Duluth likewise has gained in wheat receipts from 18,002,583 bushels in 1901 to 41,465,290 bushels in 1902 and 34,008,376 bushels in 1903. On the contrary, Chicago has been handling a steadily diminishing volume of
wheat. From 43,391,337 bushels in 1901 to 38,007.346 bushels in 1902 and 34,761,870 bushels in 1903 is evidence of the change that is gradually taking place in the course of the country's grain trade.
Chicago will, of course, be always one of the most important trade centres for wheat, corn and flour, because it is at the outlet of the corn and soft wheat belt Our Canadian railways are drawing a good deal of the trade from Chicago, and let us hope that when we have carried out contemplated improvements we will draw to Canada more and. more of that western trade. But, again, Lake Superior, is the natural outlet of our Canadian North-west, and the great trade from the American states is being diverted gradually towards Lake Superior. That is the clearest evidence of the strategic importance of Duluth in a commercial sense. Lake Superior is the key of the St. Lawrence route. It is the first link in the great water-way through Canadian channels from the west to the east. From the very beginning of civilization on this continent, the waters between Montreal and the upper lakes were recognized as the natural trade route. In 1798 the North-west Company built the first lock at Sault Ste. Marie to be used by the fur traders in French bateaux and in English boats. That first lock was 38 feet long by eight feet wide, and Mr. Clergue has renovated that interesting relic as a curiosity for those who visit Sault Ste. Marie. I feel that it is unnecessary to say much in support of the superiority of waterways as a means of transportation. That is self-evident, but the two transportation systems, the railways and the waterways are not enemies; they are allies. They must be made to work in harmony. There lias been a very severe struggle- between the railways and the waterways in the United States. In 1861 the lakes were carrying the greatest quantity of grain and flour, but in 1865 the railways began to encroach on the lake vessels for the carriage of these products, and especially flour. In 1881 Qie railways were carrying 96 per cent of all the flour transported, and had practically the whole trade in their hands. From that date, however, the lake vessels increased their flour shipments year after year, and to-day they are carrying 40 per cent of the flour from Chicago, as well as a large quantity of corn and a larger quantity of wheat. A great deal of that trade is carried to Buffalo. Chicago has lost ground. I was not in the House when the Minister of Agriculture made his excellent speech, but I notice that he gave figures to show that a large quantity of grain, and flour especially, as well as other products, were being carried from Chicago. Chicago will always be a large centre of trade, as I have said, and the many railways that are centreing there will always bring to it a trade in grain and flour. But it is undoubtedly a fact that Chicago is losing its grain

trade year after year, and for tire excellent reason that the wheat fields of some years ago are being displaced, and that the northern states are to-day the wheat-growing states par excellence. Chicago is exceptionally well located as far as railways are concerned. The distances are favourable to Chicago. The distance from Chicago to Buffalo by rail is a little over 500 miles, and the distance by lake is 889 miles. In spite of that, the lake vessels are carry ing from Chicago to-day about 40 per cent of the flour and 70 per cent of the wheat, not quite 70 per cent but over 60 per cent of the wheat. The same thing may be said of Milwaukee. In 1900 only 12 per cent of the flour from Milwaukee was shipped by rail; 39 per cent was shipped by the transit lines and 50 per cent all lake. Let us not lose sight of the fact that a large quantity of the traffic which is represented as being carried all rail is destined for local points for local consumption. Nearly all of the grain, especially of the wheat and corn, which is destined for export is carried by lake. The railways must necessarily carry grain to ports that are not reached by the lakes, and that is the reason that such a large quantity of rail traffic still appears to the credit of Chicago. I have insisted on these points to establish, to the best of my ability, the superiority of water transportation.
Let me quote on that point from the report of the proceedings of a conference that has been held in the month of June of this year. I will quote the words of Mr. Alfred Noble, who is president of the American Society of Civil Engineers :
The average haul during the season of 1902 on the lakes has been 827-4 miles. The freight was 0-89 mills per ton mile.
If the freight had been carried by rail the average could hardly have been less than three mills per ton-mile.
On this basis, the saving in transportation by the water route during one year was nearly $63,000,000. This amount of saving on Lake Superior commerce alone-, during a single year, is within $5,000,000 of the entire amount appropriated by the United States for all harbours and waterways on the lakes above Niagara Falls from the formation of the government ; if the commerce between Lake Michigan and Lake Erie be included, the annual saving greatly exceeds the amount thus appropriated. Indeed, the savings during one year on a single article, iron ore, would repay all the money expended up to this time on the waterways and harbours which it traverses on its way from mine to furnace. Viewed in this way, no great investment was ever made by a corporation or government with such a magnificent showing of profit. But a far broader view may be taken justly ; this water route has not merely afforded inexpensive transportation, but has been creative of a large part of the wealth of the nation. Without it, the development of our manufactures of iron and steel and other industries dependent on them, related to them, all constituting a great share of the national wealth, would have been retarded or impracticable ; without it, Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT. I
the prairies of the North-west would have remained unproductive and unpeopled for a much longer time. With these broad considerations in view, we may place to the credit of lake transportation a sum perhaps hardly definable, but compared to which the largest above mentioned is a mere trifle.
My hon. friend the Minister of tbe Interior has quoted some rates from Kansas City to Chicago. I did not intend to say anything at all on the question of rates which has been so fully dealt with by many members of this House, but in view of the statements made by the hon. minister, I shall refer briefly to this question. The rates on wheat from Chicago, Duluth, Port Arthur and Fort William to Meaford, Midland, Owen Sound, Goderich and other lake ports this season are between 1J and li cents and even 1 cent. The highest rate between Chicago and Buffalo in 1902, has been 2i cents. The lowest rate has been If cents, an average for the season of 1-5 cents. Let me compare the rates by rail and canal. The average rate from Chicago to New York by lake and canal in 1900-and the rates were about the same last year-was 4-49 cents ; by lake and rail, 5-10 cents ; by all-rail, 9-96 cents ; The comparison is worth noting.
In 1901 by lake and canal between the same points, that is from Chicago to New York, the rates were as follows :	By lake
and canal, 5T1 cents; by lake and rail, 5'54 cents ; by all-rail, 9-88 cents.
The Duluth rates are the same. I could quote from the reports of the Chicago Board of Trade and of the New York Produce Exchange, but I will not worry the House with quotations of rates which are available to any one who wants to look them up. They all prove in the clearest possible manner that the difference between railway transportation and lake transportation is about 60 per cent in favour of lake transportation, at least 60 per cent.
So far I have quoted the rates of to-day, the rates that have been in force. What are going to be the rates of the future ?

For about five cents a bushel of corn or wheat is carried from Chicago to New York. We should not forget that Chicago is only 912 miles from New York and about 800 miles from Baltimore and Philadelphia, so that it is in an exceptionally favourable position for railway transportation. What are going to be the rates In the future ? As I have said, grain is carried at the rate of five cents per bushel to-day between Duluth, Chicago, New Yprk, Philadelphia and Boston. Our American friends do not mean to stand idle. They do not intend to rest on the laurels they have gained. The legislature of the state of New York has adopted a project

by which $100,000,000 will be spent on the Erie Canal. That canal was started as a ditch. It began with four feet depth, when Governor DeWinton opened it- in 1825, and was only able to carry vessels of seventy-five tons capacity. It was subsequently improved and is to-day seven feet deep. A few years ago the state legislature voted a pretty large amount to deepen it to nine feet. The work was stopped because it was found too expensive, but last year the legislature voted $100,000,000 to deepen it to twelve feet. If. the electorate of the state of New York ratifies the vote of the legislature, the canal [DOT] will then be able to accommodate barges of a thousand tons capacity. The average rate on a bushel of wheat in the Erie canal to-day is 2-J cents ; and it is estimated that when the improvements to which I have just alluded, are carried out, the cost of carrying a bushel of wheat will be reduced to one-half cent or one cent per bushel. Then where will you be ? It costs one and a-half cent from Chicago, from Duluth, from Fort William and the Georgian Bay ports to Buffalo, to carry a bushel of wheat. It has cost so far three cents or three cents and a-half in the summer to carry a bushel of wheat by rail to Buffalo and two and a half cents by the Erie canal. If the rates should be reduced to one-half or one cent between Buffalo and New York, I ask again where you are going to be and what you are going to do ? Our American friends have improved their organization on the lakes in a marvellous manner. I had the advantage of making a round trip on the lakes last year. I visited nearly all the American harbours on those inland waters. I was amazed at the energy and activity that the Americans have displayed. Their organization is simply perfect. We must not be surprised at the great volume of lake trade. Lake vessels have been built with great rapidity. In 1881 the number of American vessels on the lakes was 4,000. In 1890 that number had increased to 10,555. In .1899 the number of American vessels in the lakes had risen to 20,255, and at this moment, if I am not mistaken, the number of American vessels on the lakes is 22,000. They have improved the St. Mary river and the Detroit river and deepened it to a depth of nineteen feet. Their vessels carry to-day, thanks to those improvements, as much as 250,000 bushels of grain. The size is increasing year by year. The Americans are contemplating adding an additional foot of depth on the St. Mary and Detroit rivers. Instead of nineteen feet, they will have twenty feet, which means an addition of ten per cent to the capacity of their large ships. Those waterways, the St. Mary river, the Detroit river, and the lakes, are buoyed and lighted up as the streets of Montreal and Toronto. Ships of the largest tonnage can navigate those channels just as safely at night as in the day
time. The result of their improvement has been simply marvellous. I have just given the number of ships that are navigating those waters. They number 22,000 now and the rates have been decreased from year to year as fast as the improvements have taken place. When there were only fifteen feet of water from Lake Superior to Lake Erie, the freight rates, for instance, on iron were $2 per ton. As soon as there were nineteen feet depth, the rate fell to $1 per ton. In every port of any importance, there are elevators of the most modern kind. Duluth and Lake Superior ports are gaining rapidly on Chicago, as wheat and flour centres. Duluth and West Superior have twenty-two elevators, with a capacity of 34,000,375 bushels. Buffalo has twenty-eight elevators, with a capacity of 21,390,000 bushels. St. Paul and Minneapolis have forty-two elevators, of a capacity of 34,475,000. In connection with those elevators, there are flour mills in Duluth, West Superior, Minneapolis, St. Paul, Chicago, Buffalo-in fact in all the harbours worthy of mention. Those elevators are not all of the elevating kind, but there are storage elevators, which are used in connection with elevating machinery. I think that the best elevators in the United States are at Duluth. How are those storage elevators used ? All the grain from the west cannot possibly be shipped in two or three months. Shipments of grain begin in September and terminate in December at the outside. The reason why the Americans have equipped Duluth, Chicago, West Superior, St. Paul with these elevators of more than a million of bushels capacity each, is because they have realized that they cannot possibly ship all their grain in two or three months. They ship all the grain they can in the season of navigation, then they store in their elevators all the grain that the different railways carry from their wheat fields. A good deal of that grain is used for milling purposes. A certain quantity is shipped to the seaboard, but very little. Let me remind all those who take some interest in the transportation question, that very little grain is handled in the winter months. Let my hon. friends look at the reports of the Chicago and Duluth boards of trade and the New York Exchange, and they will find that the largest quantity of grain is handled in the summer months, especially September and October. The grain that is shipped in the summer season is shipped to the different ports. We speak often of New York, Boston and Portland. But let us not forget that Philadelphia, Baltimore and Newport News are also very important reshipping points indeed. In the winter months, as soon as the season of navigation is opened, the railways raise their rates. I said a moment ago that the rates between Buffalo and New York were between three cents and three and one-half cents during

the season of navigation. But the very day the season of navigation closes the rates go up to five cents.
Mr. ItOOHE (Halifax). Will my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) permit me to ask him a question V
Certainly.
Does that refer to wheat or to corn V Corn shipped from American ports is generally grown south, and shipped earlier than wheat, which grows further north.

Chicago is the most important centre, of course, and rates are about the same for corn as for wheat, and they are about what 1 have quoted. There may be a fraction of difference at times, but the rates are just about as I have given them.
Well, Sir, bearing these facts and figures in mind, bearing in mind the plain and undeniable fact that grain is carried by our American competitors for the rates I have quoted, what is our position and what are we going to do '? My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) lias built up an argument by quoting the rates between Kansas city and Chicago. He told us that wheat had been carried for five cents per bushel between these two points.
Five cents per hundred pounds '!

Yes. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sifton) has made a mistake, unwillingly no doubt. The regular rates between Kansas city and Chicago are nineteen cents per 100 pounds. Let me say immediately that the rates from points on the western Canadian side and the American side are about the same. A good deal has been said in this parliament as to the hign rates charged by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern. Without quoting the figures, let me say, in a general way, that the rates are practically the same for the same distance. Or rather, I should say that the American railways, the Northern Pacific and the Great Northern, for instance, have a shorter haulage than the Canadian Pacific Railway has. Yet, their rates for that shorter haulage are about the same as the rates of the Canadian Pacific Railway for about double the haul.
If the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir. Tarte) wiil permit me, may 1 ask if he is speaking of the through rates from the west or the local rates V

I speak of the rates from the wheat fields of the American west and of the Canadian west to the outlet on the lakes. The rates are about the same. Well, I ask again, what are we going to do ? Are we able to compete with our American friends ? In my humble opinion we can, by taking the proper means. If Hon. Mr. TARTE.
we want to compete with them, I think we must take our lessons from them and from our own experience. Some of our hon. friends on the other side of the House have often told us and some have repeated the statement during this debate, that the present cabinet never did much for transportation. Well, I am, to a certain extent responsible for what has been done and what has not been done. All that I wanted done has not been done. I will refer to that later on. But the question of what we have not done is, after all, of less importance that the question of what we ought to do. In what position are we ? We are joint owners of the great lakes, except Lake Michigan. Now, here are some figures showing relative distances :

Sir, nothing is better fitted to educate us than facts. Let us see what Mr. Booth is doing to-day. Mr. Booth is a simple individual, a gentleman of large means, but he is only one man. He has built a railway. He started it as a colonization railway, and a railway to serve his own lumber business, but to-day he is carrying a vast amount of grain. I shall never forget an occasion when I was making an address at a banquet in the city of Montreal. My neighbour to the left happened to be a railway magnate. I had studied with some care tiie location of Mr. Booth's road and had given a good deal of attention to our geographical position. In my address I said that in my opinion Mr. Booth's road was destined to a great futrue, that it would before long carry millions and millions of bushels of grain. I was interrupted by my

neighbour in a voice loud enough to be heard ' rot.' I kept cool, but I felt that 1 would have my revenge by and by. A couple of years after, Mr. Booth published a statement saying that he had handled 20 million bushels of grain by the Canada Atlantic Railway. I took the statement to the railway magnate, one of my best friends, and I said to him ' rot.' He asked me what I meant, and I reminded him of his interruption. Mr. Booth is competing to-day with the great American railways, not only for the grain trade and the flour trade, but for trade of all kinds. He has a fleet on the iakes of six boats ; four are under American register, for the good reason that he is handling not only Canadian trade but a larger volume of American trade, and is consequently obliged to use American registered boats. Mr. Booth will carry this year over twenty million bushels of grain from Depot Harbour. He would handle fifty million bushels of corn and wheat if he could get accommodation in Montreal or elsewhere. That simple but eloquent fact is the strongest evidence of what we are capable of doing if we only do the right thing and do it now.
Lake Superior is the headquarters of the trade, but at the same time all the lakes are tributary to the St. Lawrence route. The distance from Milwaukee, from Chicago, from Duluth is shorter to Canadian ports, to the port of Montreal, than to the ports of Buffalo and New York ; in other words, a bushel of grain can be carried cheaper from those ports to the Georgian Bay ports than it can be carried to the port of Buffalo-It cannot be carried, at any rate, at the same rate, because the distance is longer than by our route. Depot Harbour is not the only harbour on the Georgian bay, all the harbours on the Georgian bay can be trade centres for grain and traffic. There are to-day, Midland, Colling-wood, Meaford. Owen Sound, and on Lake Huron, Goderich-all these harbours are reservoirs of grain. A large quantity of grain is carried, not only from Canadian points but especially from American points, to these Canadian harbours. Why is it so ? Because they are located in such a way that they offer more advantages. If they were equipped as the American harbours are equipped, they would handle a great deal more trade.
To help us to compete with the Americans we have two systems :	The all-water system through our lakes and canals, and the lake and rail system. I had the honour of being Minister of Public Works six years and a half. A year ago last January, I presented to the right hon. gentleman, then my leader, and to my colleagues, a memorandum which was the result of my investigations on the transportation question. Before the estimates were discussed I thought it my duty to place before my colleagues a report expressing my views, and giving
the result of the attention I bad bestowed upon the transportation question. I then advised my colleagues to take up energetically the question of the waterways from the head of Lake Superior down to the sea. Starting by the all-water system I advised the equipment of Fort William and the further equipment of Port Colborne. Fort William and Port Arthur are the natural and necessary outlets of our North-west domain. It would be necessary in my humble opinion to spend a pretty large amount of money to place those two harbours in a proper condition to handle trade.
The Department of Public Works is carrying out a certain amount of work now. The Mission river, which is the outlet of the Kaministiquia river to the lake should immediately be widened and deepened to a depth of 20 feet for the reason that the ice accumulates at the entrance of Port Arthur harbour. By deepening the Mission river we would certainy get two or three weeks' additional navigation in the fall months which would mean a good deal indeed. I suppose a half a million dollars could accomplish that particular work at Fort William. I beg to call the attention of my former colleagues to the statement I am making now. I have studied the question carefully,
I have been to the spot on several occasions and let me tell them that 1 know what I am talking about. Then, following our way down the lakes, I would say that all the waters should be overhauled. We should have on the lakes testing machines, as we have on the St. Lawrence, so as to be sure that we have the depth of water that we say we have in our reports, and so as to be sure that there is no obstacle to navigation. At Port Colborne a couple of million dollars should be spent, and I will tell the House how, in my humble opinion, it should be spent. The Public Works Department is completing the breakwater on the north side of the harbour. That breakwater will not be sufficient. That port cannot be used by ships for loading and unloading unless there is another breakwater on the other side. The waves on Lake Erie are nearly as big as on the Atlantic ocean, and unless you protect the ships you cannot possibly handle the trade there. I was advising my colleagues in the memo, which I hold in my hand, that an elevator and warehouses ought to be built at Port Colborne, and that the port should be equipped as a national harbour. Before I started for the Paris exhibition my colleagues were good enough to permit me to place in the estimates of the Department of Public Works the sum of $250,000 for an elevator at the port of Montreal. I had advised, and my advice had been accepted by my former colleagues, the building of an elevator at Port Colborne, at the port of Montreal and at I.Ovis. I Will explain later on why I gave thnt advice then. At Port Colborne we should ' immediately make the necessary expenditure

to provide a harbour that would allow the large boats in the carrying trade on ,tlie lakes to load and unload. On the American side, Buffalo, with its 22 elevators, with its magnificent improvements, with its good and safe harbour; on the Canadian side, nothing. We are in that position. We are public carriers. We have spent $80,000,000 in building our system of canals. It is not surprising that we are not handling more trade in our canals. We have no equipment. It would be necessary to spend a couple of million dollars to make Port Colborne what it should be. There is an obstacle at that point to which I have called the attention of the House. When a ship loaded too heavily to go through the Welland canal arrives at the entrance it is obliged to light its cargo. The Grand Trunk Railway Company has a small elevator at Port Colborne and another one at Port Dalhousie. The Grand Trunk Railway charges 2 cents a bushel to carry grain for 27 miles ; in other words, it costs more to carry a bushel of grain between these two points, 27 miles apart, than it costs to take it from Chicago to Buffalo, Port Colbourne or to Depot Harbour. That state of affairs should be put an end to immediately. The government should either acquire that piece of railway or take some means to give relief to the trade. If we want our water-ways to compete with the American water-ways we must take means to bring about that result. The distance between Port Colborne and Montreal is 807 miles, out of which there are 63 miles of canals, and the balance is composed of lake navigation. As I have said, that part of our Canadian system of navigation should be overhauled with the greatest care. The Department of Railways and Canals has had charge in the past of these water-ways.
I do not want to make any unfair reproach, but I know that our water-ways have not been overhauled and taken care of as they should have been taken care of. The government should overhaul them without delay. The channels should be made wider, they should be made deeper-, and they should be made as safe as American waters are. Now, we have reached the port of Montreal.
I advised my former colleagues in the same memo, to make in that important harbour the necessary expenditure to make it free as far as it is possible to do so. Montreal is not a local port. It is the head of navigation. It is the centre where the trade from the lakes accumulates and it is also the centre where ocean navigation comes up. AVe have, in the port of Montreal, been borrowing money on which the harbour commissioners have paid interest so far. The trade is increasing and there is no doubt whatever that the harbour commissioners will be able to continue to pay their interest. They will honour the obligations that they are incurring. There is no doubt as to that, but that is not the point. If by not making the port of Montreal as free as Hon. Mr. TARTE.
it can be made, we oblige the trade to pay tolls, that is an impediment in the way of the development of our trade. The debt of the port of Montreal, with the advance that parliament has allowed this year, will reach the very large amount of $10,000,000. Bet me ask my former colleagues in the House to weigh my humble words. This is a mistake that parliament Is committing. The St. Lawrence route, if we want to compete with the American route, must be made as free and as cheap as it is possible to make it. I do not mean to say that there shall be no charges at all in our national harbours. But we should only exact tolls sufficient to enable us to pay the cost of maintenance and nothing more. Let us make our national ports free as we have made the canals free. It would be necessary to spend in the port of Montreal at least $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 to properly equip that port. The warehouses that must be built, if we want to handle trade, will certainly cost $3,000,000. The wharfs that are being built to-day are not sufficient to give accommodation. The Grand Trunk Railway, the Canada Atlantic Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway will tell you that they cannot direct more trade to the port of Montreal because they have no accommodation there. That fact is indisputable. I had advised my colleagues in that memo, to expend the money necessary to build an elevator, to build new wharfs, to equip the port with cranes and every other modern implement that we find in every well equipped harbour in the world. Since that memo, was handed to the right hon. gentleman, the harbour commissioners of Montreal, under the direction of the Department of Public Works, have started to build an elevator with borrowed money. Sir, the government should lose no time in assuming the debt of the port of Montreal to the extent at any rate of every future expenditure including the advance that has been made this year. 1 am not speaking from a Montreal standpoint ; I am speaking from the standpoint of the St. Lawrence route from beginning to end.
In speaking of the elevators in the west I forgot to mention that it cost four cents a bushel to store grain the whole winter season in Duluth, Chicago, Minneapolis and St. Paul. I make this statement now because it will be necessary to refer to it later on.
AVe should not, I say, lose any time in carrying out the necessary policy to make the port of Montreal as free as it can be made. Let us not borrow any money. Let the government assume not only the debt, but the management of the port of Montreal. Alontreal is the terminal of our Canadian canal system. Is it reasonable that this country, having spent $80,000,000 on canals, and spending large sums of money to-day to equip our harbours on the lakes and to deepen and widen the St. Lawrence

river; is it reasonable that the terminals should not be in our own hands ? Is it a good policy ? I have nothing to say against the Montreal harbour commissioners, but I do say that the system is bad,' I have been long enough a minister to know that the system is thoroughly inefficient. Twelve or thirteen men meet there a couple of hours a week ; business men who have their occupations waiting for them. They discuss matters in a very light way at times. I do not make any personal allusions, for I speak of the past commissioners just as I do of the present ones. The work costs at least 30 per cent more than it should cost, and the work is not attended to as it should be. There is nobody responsible. I am speaking within hearing of friends from Montreal who know that I am speaking the truth, and not all the truth either. The commissioners are men of good-will, but they are not competent for that kind of business. A minister is responsible to this parliament; the government is responsible to this House; you can lay your hand on them when they make a mistake, but the harbour commissioners are irresponsible, and you cannot do anything with them. They do the best they can, but I repeat that they are not competent to handle a large proposition like the most important harbour of this country. Last year the trade of the Montreal harbour reached the wonderful amount of $191,000,000, being nearly half the total trade of this country. Is it reasonable that such a harbour should not be under the control of the nation itself? ,
I had advised my colleagues to equip the ports of Three Rivers and Quebec; the St. Lawrence route for me is all the one thing. I had advised the building of elevators at Three Rivers and at Levis. The government lias reduced the plans that my department, under my direction, had prepared for the harbour works at Quebec. I believe they made a mistake in reducing these plans, but nevertheless they are doing a useful work. In Quebec they are perhaps a little better off than we are in Montreal; they are, of course, not handling the vast quantity of trade that Montreal handles, but nevertheless the port of Quebec is not eqpip-ped as it should be.
I had also advised the beginning of what is called the Georgian Bay canal. I do not advise the whole project immediately, but I did advise the immediate improvement of the French river. The distances have not perhaps been given the attention that they should receive, and I propose to state what they are here. From Fort William to Buffalo tlie distance is 750 miles, and from; Fort William to North Bay the distance is 543 miles, difference in favour of North Bay of 207 miles. The distance from Duluth to Buffalo is 857 miles, and from Duluth to North Bay 575 miles, a distance in favour of North Bay of 282 miles. The
distance from Milwaukee to Buffalo is 716 miles, and from Milwaukee to North Bay 463 miles, a difference in favour of North Bay of 253 miles. The distance from Chicago to Buffalo is 733 miles, and from Chicago to North Bay 520 miles, a difference of 213 miles in favour of North Bay.
That work from the mouth of the French river to North Bay would cost in the neighbourhood of $5,000,000. It has been represented to me on several occasions that the distance to Midland, another Georgian Bay port, is about the same as to North Bay, and there is something in that point.

friend the Prime Minister himself to the immediate necessity of better buoying and better lighthouses and better fog signals on the St. Lawrence from the straits of Belle Isle up. Let me tell him that after the numerous trips I have made on the St. Lawrence route from Belle Isle up, 1 have come to the conclusion that the St. Lawrence route has not been attended to as it should have been and that it is not to day receiving the attention it should. The Prime Minister himself should take that matter in hand. The Department of Marine and Fisheries should be strengthened.
Oh, oh.

Well, I mean strengthened as far as officials are concerned. We had better have strong officials ; let us have officials who would listen to instead of resisting arguments. I have nothing to say against the present officials. I know one thing, that when the minister does not travel himself he is making a mistake. Now, we have accidents-we will have accident after accident, unless better attention is given to the St. Lawrence. The pilotage system should be attended to without any delay ; it is bad. The St. Lawrence, I say it again, is not attended to as it should be and what is the result 1 The result is that the insurance rates are higher from the ports of Montreal and Quebec than from American ports. There is no great danger between Quebec and Montreal ; if a boat grounds it only scratches its bottom a little, that is all. But if unfortunately a boat is grounded in the gulf, well, the scratch is a little deeper, the ship is lost and then up go the insurance rates.	.
We should have a system of elevators at Port Colborne. at Montreal and at Levis. How do the Americans handle their business ? First let me remind the House and the Prime Minister, there is not one single American transcontinental line which goes from ocean to ocean. They go to the Pacific ocean but their terminals are at Omaha. St. Paul, Duluth and Chicago. They carry the products of the west, of the wheat belt and the corn belt, to the outlet. They load their elevators with this grain that they hare not been able to carry in the summer months, during the seasons of navigation. In winter the manufactures mill it and flour and grain are carried to the seaports : New York, Boston, Portland, Newport News, Philadelphia and Baltimore, and a certain quantity of grain to fill the boats. My hon. friends from the maritime provinces will perhaps be kind enough to give some attention to what I am now saying. When I was Minister of Public Works I always endeavoured to study their case and their position to the best of my ability.
Now, what are the Americans doing ? They carry grain to Buffalo, to Duluth, to Chicago and in winter months they ship it to their winter ports. Between Buffalo and

New York the distance is 440 miles by the New York Central ; between Levis and St. John it is only 578 miles on the Intercolonial and it will be only 500 miles on the new railway which my hon. friends are asking the House to allow them to build. We will be able to compete with our American friends if we carry the wheat by our waterways as the Americans are doing. What I suggested nearly two years ago not only stands good to-day, but stands better than it did then. Our policy must be a policy of cheap rates, otherwise we will not be able to compete. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior was reminding us the other day that a few steps from the Canadian frontier the American system of railways is working. My hon. friend is perfectly right and the distance between Winnipeg and American ports is not very great. From Winnipeg to St. Paul is only 500 miles ; from Winnipeg to Duluth is only 450 miles ; from Winnipeg to Port Arthur is 440 miles by the Canadian Northern Railway and 425 miles by the Canadian Pacific Railway. From Chicago to New York is only 912 miles. Now we have to be careful. For if we do not provide cheap means to carry our traffic the Americans will get it in the future as they have done in the past. St. John and Halifax, our Canadian winter ports, will get more grain and flour traffic by the waterways than they ever will by any all-rail project. What the Americans have accomplished is clear evidence of what we could do.	Let us not lose sight
of one thing. We have to compete, not only as regards distances, but we have to compete against strongly entrenched rivals. Those ports of New York, Boston, Philadelphia and Baltimore are great centres of trade. The railways are always sure to get there return cargoes, but the ports of St. John and Halifax have not so far been pro-. Stable centres in that respect. The Canadian Pacific Railway have taken a good quantity of traffic but the east-bound traffic has been always about ten times larger than the west bound traffic. Of course, conditions will improve and they will improve more if we take the means to give to our harbours and winter ports better equipment. Let us equip the St. Lawrence route in the way I am now suggesting. Let us accumulate a grain trade in the St. Lawrence in the fall months, and Halifax and St. John will have more trade to handle. There will always be a certain quantity of through trade handled in the winter months. Cattle will be handled by rail, and the winter months are fairly good for that trade. These are in resume my views on the question of waterways and transportation. I think that there is urgent necessity for us to apply o'Ur energy and our financial means to improving our waterways immediately, otherwise we will lose trade. Holding these views, I awaited with a great deal of interest and anxiety the ministerial explanation on the project before us. I

stand in this happy position that I have no party purposes to serve. I am speaking for myself and without any bias or prejudice.
What is the project we have to discuss to-day ? The Grand Trunk Railway applied during this session for a charter from Quebec to the Pacific ocean. When the Bill was discussed before the Railway Committee, Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson and Mr. Hays positively declined to agree to build the eastern section at the same time as the portion in the North-west Territories. Their views was to build a railway from Gravenhurst or North Bay to the Territories. We had a vote on those points. The Grand Trunk Railway positively, declined to agree to build the eastern portion of this project simultaneously. X quite understand that position in which the government was placed.
I am not going to impute to them any improper motives. That is not my way of discussing questions of broad policy. I quite understand their position. When the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway declined to build the eastern portion, the government were urged by their followers to build the eastern portion from Quebec to the west ? Then our friends from the maritime provinces appeared on the scene and insisted on having the line extended to their territory. The government could not induce the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to take up the scheme. The Minister of Trade and Commerce told us to-day very frankly that the Grand Trunk Railway credit could not build the whole enterprise, and in that my right hon. friend was right. No private company could safely build that part of the project. Then the government made up their minds to build it themselves. Let me say here that I do not share the views of those who believe that there are not good agricultural lands in the territories through which this road will go. I cannot possibly agree in the views expressed on that point. I happen to know some parts of that country well. I lived eighteen years in the city of Quebec and took special interest in the Lake St. John district. That was a great colonization district, and at its inception X took a great interest in connection with my newspaper in that part of the province. I can assure the House that from Roberval towards the west there is a magnificent fertile district, splendid lands, lands just as good as any in this country. I see some of my hon. friends nodding no, but let me tell them that I am speaking of what I know. I had properties there, not very extensive, and X have been out there fifty times at least so that I know the country pretty well.
I know that part of the country well, and it was because I* know it well that I urged, with tlie help of my right hon. friend-that we urged upon our colleagues in 1900 to give to the Lake St. John Railway Company a subsidy on sixty miles, from Roberval towards James Bay. I think the government would have done well to increase the distance covered by that subsidy and also^ to increase the rate of subsidy itself, for 33,200 per mile cannot possibly build a road there.
It is a fine district. The Lake Temiskam-angue district is also a very fine country.
I was there some years ago, and I was there again last year. It is a fine district, capable of giving to settlers all the advantages that the best lands can give. The region of Lake Nipissing is also a good district. There are fertile belts, there is no doubt about that, and there are also barren lands. Behind Quebec, on the Ste. Anne river there are some lots fit for colonization, but there is no very great extent of good land. In my younger days I have often been on hunting and fishing expeditions over the height of land, across the Laurentian range. X know that part of the country fairly well. The road will pass through a country, so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, in which there are large stretches of cultivable land. Below Quebec, I happen to know the country. Mv hon. friend from Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) made a statement as to the region below Quebec through which the line will pass. I have had the honour to represent L'lslet in this House, and I know the parishes through which the road will pass. They are very, very fine settlements. The whole of that district is good land. The settlers to-day are at a distance of from thirty to forty miles from the Intercolonial Railway. As to this part of the project, I believe that it is wrong to say that the-lands are not good. We have no interest in saying that the lands that we possess are not good when they are good. I will not discuss the project of the government on those lines. Now, having said that much, I will discuss the question from another standpoint.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister, in introducing this Bill, told us that the project was imperative, that it was necessary not to lose any time. Well, I shall not say that we have no survey, no information at all, but I would ask my right hon. friend whether we could not have had more information than we have now, whether before embarking on this project it would not have been the part of prudence to get more information? We know that there are good lands through which this road will pass, but no survey has been made for the construction of a railway. We do not know what obstacles are to he met. Nobody knows. Then, nobody knows the financial aspect of the project. It is very well to say that the road will not cost more than $35,000 or $30,000 a mile, but I ask my right hon. friend whether he is sure that it will not cost more ? I am not afraid of spending money. In point of fact I have been accused of being a spender of money. But I find myself a very moderate man indeed in the face of the schemes of the leaders on either side of this House. It is evident that I am not so progressive as these hon. gentle-

men are. Why was this scheme imperative? Was it from a transportation point of view ? I do not think it was imperative, and when my right hon. friend thinks it over, I believe he will agree with me. The road will be useful. I am glad, for one, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company gets into the North-west. I should like to see them there for good. I will deal with the position of the Grand Trunk later on. But the government have resolved to build a railway from Winnipeg to Moncton. For local purposes, it will be a useful road. I never knew of a railway that was not useful. It will develop the part of the country through which it passes-there is no doubt about that. The questions are, first, what would be the cost ? And, second, could we have done better ? As to the project being imperative, I think that the House has made up its mind that it is not so urgent as my right hon. friend said it was. It is not imperative, but the project is an attractive one from certain standpoints. This road will not afford us the means of competing for the trade of the west. It will not cheapen the rates on wheat or any other commodity by a fraction of a cent. Nobody on either side has tried to show that the rates will be made cheaper. It is simply out of the question that the road can have that effect. Let us compare the figures. Mr. Wolvin, to-day is taking grain from Duluth and Chicago to Quebec for less than 3 cents in the summer months. This road will not carry grain at that rate, will it ? It is out of the question. The season of navigation lasts for more than seven months. On the American side very little grain is handled in the winter months. Some is brought down during those months, just as some is brought down over the all-rail route of the Canadian Pacific Railway. But nobody pretends that this new road will cheapen the rates by a single fraction of a cent. No business man, in this House will contradict me on that point. From that standpoint, then, the scheme is not imperative. Would it have been better for the government not to make an arrangement with the Grand Trunk ? What is going to be the result of our policy? The government has made the agreement, and, of course, the House will support the proposal of the government. For that proposal was submitted to a ministerial caucus, and it must be carried now. We may as well discuss things as they are. The scheme is to be carried-it will be carried. There are members of parliament who are not enthusiastic, but, of course, party government is party government.
Hear, hear.

Yes, and when my Conservative friends are on this side of the House the government will be a party government, as it always has been. We are here to talk business, and not to make theories. Well, now, we have no infor-Hon. Mr. TARTE.
mation, the government has no more information than I have to enable them to reach a definite conclusion as to the cost. It may cost $40,000 a mile, it may cost more. The Grand Trunk Pacific is going to pay 3 per cent interest after seven years, and is exempted for three years more in certain contingencies-I think we may safely call it ten years. When the ten years are over, if the road is not paying, then the government will be approached by the Grand Trunk Pacific and will be urged not to exact interest. That is the ordinary course of affairs. It is just as well to look these things in the face. We are undertaking an enterprise that will certainly involve the credit of the country for a large amount of money. It is 1,500 miles from Winnipeg to Quebec, if that cos'ts $40,000 a mile-it may cost more than that- there will be $60,000,000. Add $15,000,000 for the road from Quebec to Moncton, and you have $75,000,000. Well, we must make allowance for contingencies, and I think we may say $20,000,000 without hesitation for interest, &c. We are not very far .from $100,000,000. Now, the country is rich and prosperous, and if the money is well invested we can stand it. But is it a good investment ? Are we sure ? Are my hon. friends on the treasury benches sure that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will pay interest ? They are no more sure of it than I am. We are undertaking, as I said, an enterprise that will involve the credit of the country to the extent of nearly $100,000,000. What I fear is that we are embarking in an enterprise that will prevent us from doing something else that is more necessary. If the government are sure, if my hon. friends who support the government do feel confident that the government are making a safe calculation, I think their duty is to join me in using ail legitimate constitutional pressure on my right hon. friend and his colleagues to induce them to go on with our waterway development immediately. We cannot cheapen transport by the new project, we cannot cheapen rates for our western territories. With the waterways w.e can certainly do it, that fact is indisputable. Our friends from the maritime provinces would derive more benefit for their winter ports through a waterway policy than they will from this railway policy. They will not get any trade from this railway, they would get a vast amount of trade through a good waterway policy.
